notes:
I couldn't find any verse in Psalm 20 where Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal, Reformed, Lutheran or Anglican teachers clearly disagree along denominational lines. The real debates in the sources I read are about interpretation, mainly in vv. 6 and 9. I also found nothing from Lutheran, Orthodox or Pentecostal-specific sites, nothing from Wesley's own notes, and no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on v. 4. Those gaps are left out below.

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**Whole psalm / v. 1 (title)**
- The setting: the people pray for their king before a battle, and the king answers with confidence that God will deliver him. Guzik (Enduring Word) applies it both to David and, looking ahead, to Jesus going to the cross. Pastor David walks us through a psalm where the people of Israel pray for their king before battle, then the king responds with confidence in God's deliverance. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-20/
- Matthew Henry says it is the will of God that people pray especially for kings. He calls this psalm a prayer for the king and Psalm 21 the matching thanksgiving. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_020.cfm
- Spurgeon reads it as foretelling Christ: the ancient church crying out for her Lord as she sees, in vision, his great struggle on her behalf. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps020.cfm
- Ellicott thinks it was written for part-singing in the Temple. The congregation prays (vv. 1–5), the priest or king declares confidence (vv. 6–8), and everyone joins in the closing cry. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/20.htm

**v. 1**
- Pulpit Commentary: the people ask God to hear the king's own prayers, which he is probably praying silently while they pray aloud. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/20.htm
- Henry: even the greatest people face trouble and must pray. Others' prayers for us should back up our own prayers, not replace them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_020.cfm
- "God of Jacob": Ellicott links it to Jacob's words in Genesis 35:3 about the God who answered him in his distress. He says "defend" is better rendered "set thee up on high," as in a fortress out of the enemy's reach. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/20.htm
- Gill: the title separates the true God from false gods, and it appeals to God's covenant with Jacob's descendants. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/20-1.htm
- NET note: God's "name" stands for God himself and the qualities his name suggests. Here it stresses his relationship to Israel. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=psa+20

**v. 2**
- "Sanctuary" is read two ways: heaven, or the tabernacle on Zion where the ark was, toward which Israel prayed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/20-2.htm
- Henry: the help asked for comes not from ordinary providence but from the ark of the covenant and God's special favour to Israel. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_020.cfm
- Guzik, quoting Spurgeon, suggests the verse also works as a blessing between a pastor and his people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-20/

**v. 3**
- Ellicott: the king is offering the customary sacrifices before battle, both the burnt offering (*olah*) and the grain offering (*minchah*). "Accept" literally means "make fat," that is, treat it as a worthy offering. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/20.htm
- Guzik: not every sacrifice is accepted. Offerings made without faith, or outside the Levitical system, were not. He applies the burnt offering to the cross. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-20/
- Pulpit: David would not have killed the animals himself; a priest would have done it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/20.htm
- Henry: we can know God accepts our spiritual sacrifices if his Spirit lights a holy fire of love for God in us. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/psalms/20.htm

**v. 4**
- Guzik: at that moment David wanted only to defend God's people, so the prayer was a good one. The key is to find our place in God's plan rather than trying to fit God into ours. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-20/
- Gill: the people could pray this in faith because David was a man after God's own heart. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/20-4.html
- Pulpit: it means everything the king hopes this campaign will achieve. NET: it probably means his prayer for protection and victory and his battle plan. https://biblehub.com/psalms/20-4.htm ; https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=psa+20
- Clarke: probably spoken by the high priest. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/20-4.html

**v. 5**
- Guzik: the people were so sure of God's help that they planned their victory celebration before the battle. He quotes Trapp's reading of the banners as defiance to the enemy and tokens of God's glory. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-20/
- Ellicott: better "wave our banners." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/20.htm
- Augustine and Dunwell (quoted in Spurgeon) apply "fulfil all thy petitions" to Christ's ongoing intercession for us. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801020.htm ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps020.cfm

**v. 6**
- Maclaren (Expositor's Bible): the most natural speaker is the king. Faith speaks of the future as already done, since he knows "Jehovah has saved" before any blow is struck. The answer comes from heaven, a holier sanctuary than Zion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/20.htm
- Ellicott: the confidence comes after the speaker sees the sacrifice offered and is sure it was accepted. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/20.htm
- Guzik cites Kidner: "saves" (vv. 6 and 9) comes from the same Hebrew root as the name Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-20/

**v. 7**
- Henry suggests David had the Syrians in mind, whose armies relied heavily on chariots and horsemen. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_020.cfm
- Guzik: David deliberately refused to trust in military strength, because God had told Israel's kings not to multiply horses (Deuteronomy 17:16). The "name" is not a magic word; it stands for God's whole character and his faithfulness to his covenant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-20/
- Maclaren notes the Red Sea, where the Name proved stronger than Pharaoh's chariots. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/20.htm
- Ellicott: the word "trust" is not in the Hebrew. He renders it "these in chariots… but we in the name of Jehovah our God make boast." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/20.htm

**v. 8**
- Ellicott pictures a whole battle: those knocked down get up, return to the fight and beat their enemies. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/20.htm
- Henry applies it to the last day, when believers raised from the dead will stand. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/psalms/20.htm

**v. 9**
- Guzik: the cry "Save, LORD!" comes before the battle, which shows that David's trust was real. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-20/
- Barnes: being confident does not mean they stop praying. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/20-9.htm

## 2. Where teachers differ

- **v. 6, who is "His anointed"?** Gill (labelled "Baptist · Calvinism" on StudyLight) says this is not David speaking about himself but the Messiah. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/bsb/psalms/20-6.html Ellicott says it means the king of the poem, and reading it as Israel or an "ideal" king doesn't fit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/20.htm Guzik takes both views: David first, and Jesus more fully. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-20/
- **v. 9, who is "the King"?** Barnes says it is God, the Great King. Poole lists David, God or Christ as possible and leans toward "Lord, save the king." Gill says it is the Messiah. Keil–Delitzsch and the Cambridge Bible follow the Greek (LXX) and Latin (Vulgate) translations: "O Lord, save the king," the source of "God save the King." Pulpit finds the scholars "nearly equally balanced." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/20-9.htm
- **v. 6, who says "I"?** Spurgeon's source (Ambrose) says the people speak as one voice. Pulpit says the high priest or the king. Clarke says the priest after the sacrifice. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps020.cfm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/20.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/bsb/psalms/20-6.html

## 3. Other views

- **Modern scholarship (NET notes):**
  - The verbs in vv. 1–5 could be read as confident statements ("the LORD will answer") rather than wishes.
  - In v. 5 the editors prefer to change "raise a banner" to "we will rejoice."
  - The v. 6 speaker may have just received a prophetic word promising salvation.
  - In v. 7, "some… others" are probably Israel's enemies.
  - In v. 9 they change "Save!" to "The LORD will deliver the king," taking the king as David's heir.
  https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=psa+20
- **Bible.org:** "His anointed" became a popular title for God's special coming King. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-20
- **Catholic (Augustine):**
  - The prophet is speaking *to* Christ.
  - v. 6 foretells the resurrection.
  - v. 7: chariots and horses are worldly goods and proud honours.
  - v. 8: those who fell are unbelieving Israel, while the Gentiles "rise," justified by faith.
  - v. 9: the King is the risen Priest who offers our sacrifices.
  https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801020.htm
- **Popular modern teaching (v. 4):** I found no source describing prosperity teaching here. The closest thing is a Bible Hub study note that says the verse is "not a blank check for selfish cravings," with fulfilled desire tied to delighting in God (Psalm 37:4). https://biblehub.com/psalms/20-4.htm
